excerpt: Mixed-berry trays combining raspberry, blueberry, and blackberry are commercially attractive but present packaging engineering challenges because each species has a distinct optimal modified atmosphere range and a different respiration rate at equivalent temperatures. This study evaluated 12 commercially available polymeric packaging films differing in oxygen transmission rate (OTR) and carbon dioxide transmission rate (CO₂TR) for their suitability in MAP of mixed-berry trays stored at 2 °C. Headspace equilibrium gas compositions were measured at 24-hour intervals over eight days and compared against species-specific target ranges determined from prior single-species trials. Microbiological and firmness data were collected at four-day intervals. A film with OTR of 3,800 cm³/m²/day and CO₂TR of 18,000 cm³/m²/day delivered headspace conditions within acceptable ranges for all three species simultaneously and reduced mold incidence by 55% relative to a standard polyethylene control. Finite element modelling of gas permeation through the film was used to confirm experimental headspace trends and to predict equilibrium under alternative tray fill-weight scenarios. The results provide film specification guidance for packers handling mixed-berry formats and demonstrate that a single film solution can satisfy the conflicting atmosphere requirements of co-packaged fruit species.

Rapid and uniform pre-cooling of freshly harvested raspberries prior to MAP sealing is critical for establishing the target equilibrium atmosphere within packaging. This experimental study examined three pre-cooling protocols — forced-air cooling at 2 m/s, hydrocooling at 1 °C, and room cooling as control — applied to raspberry punnets subsequently sealed under a 5% O₂/15% CO₂ MAP at 2 °C storage. Headspace gas composition was monitored at 0, 6, 12, 24, and 48 hours post-sealing using an inline gas analyzer. Fruit core temperature profiles, firmness, respiration rate (CO₂ evolution), and drip loss were recorded throughout a 10-day storage trial. Forced-air cooling achieved target core temperature in 38 minutes compared to 210 minutes for room cooling, and resulted in target headspace O₂ equilibration 14 hours earlier than the room-cooled control. Faster equilibration was associated with significantly lower Botrytis incidence (p < 0.01) and superior firmness retention at day 8. Hydrocooling achieved comparable equilibration speed but introduced elevated free moisture that promoted calyx decay. The findings quantify the shelf-life benefit of investing in forced-air cooling infrastructure and inform revised pre-cooling standard operating procedures for export packers.

This study investigated the effect of modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) on the postharvest quality and shelf life of Serbian-grown raspberries intended for export markets. Three gas compositions — 5% O₂/15% CO₂/80% N₂, 10% O₂/10% CO₂/80% N₂, and ambient air control — were evaluated at 2 °C storage over a 14-day period. Quality parameters including firmness, color (L*, a*, b*), soluble solids content, titratable acidity, and visual mold incidence were monitored at two-day intervals. Microbiological analyses targeted total aerobic counts and Botrytis cinerea colony formation. Results demonstrated that the 5% O₂/15% CO₂ atmosphere reduced Botrytis incidence by 63% relative to control and maintained firmness above commercial acceptability thresholds for 12 days compared to 6 days in ambient conditions. Sensory panel scores for color and texture confirmed marketability at day 10 under optimal MAP conditions. The findings provide actionable gas-mix specifications for exporters shipping raspberries to Central European markets, and establish a data foundation for integrating MAP parameters into predictive shelf-life models. Practical recommendations for film permeability selection and pallet-level gas management are discussed.

Static best-before labelling does not reflect the actual quality state of perishable foods subjected to variable cold-chain conditions. This paper reports a feasibility study for implementing sensor-based dynamic remaining shelf-life (RSL) labelling on raspberry and blueberry consignments exported from Serbia. Time-temperature indicator (TTI) labels from two commercial suppliers were benchmarked against data-logger-calibrated predictive model outputs for Botrytis growth and total aerobic count across 24 simulated and 16 real export consignments. TTI colour-response kinetics were characterised at 0, 4, 8, and 12 °C and integrated into an RSL calculation algorithm using an Arrhenius-based temperature dependence model. Agreement between TTI-derived RSL and model-derived RSL was within ±1.2 days for 79% of consignments, which was deemed commercially acceptable by participating exporters. A cost–benefit analysis estimated that TTI-based RSL labelling could reduce consignment rejection rates at destination by 18–24%, yielding a positive return on investment for exporters operating above 50 tonnes per season. Regulatory and labelling compliance considerations under EU food law are discussed, along with the data requirements for formal TTI validation. The study supports the case for piloting RSL labelling in the Serbian berry export sector as part of a broader cold-chain quality assurance programme.

Active packaging systems incorporating volatile antimicrobial agents derived from plant extracts represent a promising complement to conventional modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) for fresh blueberries. This study assessed the efficacy of sachets containing encapsulated thymol and carvacrol — sourced from wild thyme and oregano — integrated into clamshell packaging under a 5% O₂/15% CO₂ atmosphere at 2 °C. Blueberry quality was monitored over 18 days for firmness, total anthocyanin content, weight loss, and microbiological load (total aerobic count and Botrytis incidence). Active MAP sachets reduced total aerobic counts by 1.8 log CFU/g relative to passive MAP controls at day 12 and delayed visible mold onset by four days. Anthocyanin retention was significantly higher in active MAP treatments (p < 0.05), suggesting a secondary antioxidant protective effect. Consumer acceptability scores obtained through a 40-member sensory panel confirmed marketable quality at day 14 for saline-active MAP versus day 10 for passive MAP controls. Migration testing confirmed that thymol and carvacrol residues in fruit tissue remained below European regulatory thresholds. This work demonstrates the practical feasibility of combining MAP gas composition with natural antimicrobial active elements for export-grade blueberry packaging.

Digital twin frameworks — virtual replicas of physical supply chains updated by real-time sensor data — offer a new paradigm for proactive spoilage management in perishable food logistics. This paper describes the integration of validated predictive microbial growth models for Botrytis cinerea and total aerobic bacteria into a digital twin architecture developed for Serbian berry cold-chain operations. The system ingests temperature and relative humidity streams from IoT sensors placed within refrigerated transport units and storage rooms, feeding real-time inputs into a model library calibrated for raspberry, blueberry, and strawberry substrates. A graphical dashboard presents logistics managers with dynamically updated remaining shelf-life estimates and spoilage risk scores for each consignment. A 12-month pilot deployment covering four exporting companies and 240 consignments demonstrated that digital twin alerts correctly flagged 88% of consignments subsequently confirmed to exhibit elevated spoilage at destination. False-positive rates were 9%, attributed primarily to anomalous sensor placement near evaporator coils. Integration with enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems for automated re-routing decisions is discussed as a near-term development pathway. The study establishes a reproducible blueprint for deploying predictive microbiology within commercial cold-chain digital twin platforms in the Serbian fruit export sector.

Deterministic predictive models assume fixed temperature inputs, which rarely reflect the stochastic nature of real-world cold-chain environments. This study presents a stochastic modelling framework for predicting the remaining shelf life of fresh strawberries under realistic fluctuating temperature conditions. A Monte Carlo simulation approach was applied to propagate uncertainty in temperature distribution parameters — derived from 180 sensor-monitored consignments — through a validated secondary model for total aerobic count growth on strawberry. Output distributions of predicted shelf life were compared against observed microbiological end-point data from the same consignments. The stochastic model significantly outperformed its deterministic equivalent in capturing the spread of observed outcomes, with prediction intervals covering 91% of empirical data points. Sensitivity analysis identified mean transport temperature and frequency of door-opening events as the two variables contributing most to shelf-life variance. A simplified probabilistic shelf-life index (PSI) was derived for use by quality managers without specialist modelling expertise. The framework is applicable to other soft fruits and other pathogen or spoilage organism combinations, provided primary growth data are available. This work advances the practical deployment of quantitative risk-informed decision-making in Serbian berry export supply chains.

This book chapter provides a comprehensive treatment of the engineering principles underpinning postharvest preservation of fresh horticultural products, with emphasis on modified atmosphere packaging and cold-chain management. The chapter opens with a review of the biochemical and microbiological deterioration mechanisms that govern shelf life in soft fruits, including ethylene-mediated ripening, oxidative browning, and fungal pathogen proliferation. It then develops the engineering framework for MAP system design, covering gas mass balance modelling, film permeability selection, and tray geometry effects on headspace equilibration dynamics. Cold-chain management is addressed through the lens of predictive microbiology, explaining how primary and secondary models can be linked to temperature monitoring data to generate real-time shelf-life estimates. A section on supply chain integration discusses how MAP and predictive modelling tools can be embedded in digital logistics systems. Case studies drawn from Serbian berry export operations illustrate the translation of laboratory models into operational practice, including a worked example of a forced-air pre-cooling and MAP line for a mid-sized raspberry exporter. The chapter concludes with a forward-looking discussion of emerging active packaging technologies and AI-assisted cold-chain optimisation. It is intended for graduate students and food industry engineers seeking a practically oriented reference.

The effect of oven ageing at 80 °C for periods of 0, 7, 14, 21 and 28 days on the properties of two mLLDPE cast films was investigated to assess fitness for shelf-life-extended food packaging. Films were evaluated by DSC (crystallinity, melting peak), tensile testing (yield stress, elongation at break), and seal strength at a fixed jaw temperature of 115 °C. After 28 days, crystallinity increased by 3.1–4.7 percentage points in both grades, consistent with post-crystallisation. Yield stress rose by 8–12 %, while elongation at break declined from 620 % to 490–530 %, indicating embrittlement. Seal strength dropped by 12–17 % relative to the unaged films, attributed to increased crystallinity at the film surface reducing interdiffusion during sealing. Oxidation induction time measured by DSC-OIT at 200 °C under oxygen remained above 25 min for both grades after 28 days, indicating that the primary antioxidant package was not depleted. The results suggest a conservative shelf life of 18 months for sealed rolls stored below 35 °C.

A two-dimensional transient finite-element model of heat transfer from flat seal jaws through a multilayer OPP/tie/mLLDPE film stack was developed and validated against thermocouple measurements embedded in films at 0.1 s time resolution. Film layer thermal conductivities were taken from the literature (mLLDPE: 0.35 W/m·K; OPP: 0.22 W/m·K); jaw face temperature was set to experimentally measured values between 110 and 135 °C. Model predictions of seal-interface temperature matched experimental values with a mean absolute error of 1.8 °C across 48 test conditions. Simulations were then used to assess how jaw pressure (0.1–0.5 N/mm²) and dwell time (0.2–0.8 s) influence the time spent above the seal-initiation temperature of 97 °C at the film interface. Results show that for jaw temperatures at or below 115 °C, reducing dwell time below 0.35 s prevents the interface from reaching SIT even at maximum jaw pressure. The model provides a practical tool for setting sealing parameters without exhaustive trial runs.
Seal-Layer Blend Composition for Heat-Sealable Cast Polyolefin Films with Reduced Seal-Initiation Temperature

This paper reports a formulation development exercise carried out with a regional flexible-packaging converter. The target was to lower the required jaw temperature on a 300 bags/min VFFS line from 125 °C to below 110 °C without reducing seal strength below 25 N/25 mm or compromising hot-tack performance. Starting from a commercial 40 µm mLLDPE monolayer film, two modifications were evaluated: (i) partial substitution of the mLLDPE base resin with a 1-octene-based very-low-density polyethylene (VLDPE, density 0.900 g/cm³) at 10–25 wt%, and (ii) increasing seal-layer thickness from 40 to 50 µm in a three-layer coextrudate with OPP and tie. VLDPE addition at 20 wt% lowered SIT by 9 °C and enabled 26 N/25 mm plateau seal strength at 108 °C. Increasing film thickness to 50 µm without VLDPE gave a 5 °C SIT reduction. The combination of 20 wt% VLDPE and 50 µm gauge achieved a usable sealing window of 106–138 °C, a 32 °C range versus 18 °C for the commercial film. Line trials on a production VFFS machine confirmed seal integrity of filled pouches under 1.5 bar air pressure.

The project investigated the relationship between seal-layer formulation variables—resin type, comonomer content, blend ratios, and film thickness—and the achievable thermal processing window on VFFS packaging lines running at up to 300 bags/min. Work was conducted across four tasks: rheological and thermal characterisation of candidate resins; cast-film extrusion trials on the laboratory line at the Faculty of Technology; heat-seal testing using a gradient sealer and a laboratory VFFS unit; and statistical modelling of composition–property relationships using RSM. The project produced seven publications and validated two target formulations with an industrial partner. A trained PhD student and two master's students were involved. Equipment procured under the project included an updated hot-tack tester and an ATR-FTIR accessory.

Two standard seal-quality tests—the 180° peel test and the differential pressure burst test—were applied to heat-sealed pouches made from OPP/tie/mLLDPE films sealed across a jaw temperature range of 95–140 °C. For each jaw temperature, 20 pouches were prepared and tested by both methods. Peel force data and burst pressure data were analysed for correlation and for their ability to discriminate between adequate and inadequate seals. The two methods agreed in classifying seals above 110 °C as acceptable (peel ≥ 25 N/25 mm; burst ≥ 180 kPa), but diverged in the 100–109 °C zone, where 7 of 20 pouches passed the burst test but failed the peel criterion. Root-cause analysis by SEM cross-section showed incomplete interdiffusion at the seal interface in those pouches. Repeatability expressed as coefficient of variation was 5.8 % for peel and 9.2 % for burst across all jaw temperatures. The peel test is recommended as the more conservative acceptance criterion for VFFS applications handling liquid or particulate products.

A blend composition for the seal layer of cast polyolefin films comprising 65–80 wt% metallocene linear low-density polyethylene with 1-octene comonomer, 15–25 wt% very-low-density polyethylene with density in the range 0.895–0.905 g/cm³, and 5–10 wt% low-density polyethylene with melt flow index below 1.0 g/10 min. The composition achieves a seal-initiation temperature below 100 °C at standard jaw conditions (0.3 N/mm², 0.4 s) and a plateau seal strength above 27 N/25 mm, providing a usable sealing window of at least 30 °C. Applicable to monolayer films and as the seal layer of coextruded or laminated multilayer structures for VFFS packaging.

Three-layer films with an oriented polypropylene (OPP) structural layer, an adhesive tie layer, and an mLLDPE seal layer were produced by lamination. Seal-layer thickness was varied at 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 µm while total film gauge was held at 60 µm. Sealing experiments were conducted on a laboratory gradient heat-sealer over a 85–140 °C jaw temperature range; dwell time was fixed at 0.4 s and jaw pressure at 0.25 N/mm². Seal strength and hot-tack force were measured. Films with 20 µm seal layers achieved plateau seal strength of 31 N/25 mm and maintained hot-tack force above 6 N/25 mm over a 28 °C window (108–136 °C). Reducing the seal layer to 10 µm narrowed the hot-tack window to 16 °C and lowered plateau seal strength to 22 N/25 mm; increasing to 30 µm provided no significant benefit. Optical microscopy of cross-sections confirmed nominal thicknesses within ±1.5 µm. The 20 µm seal layer is proposed as the practical optimum for this film construction.

Seal-initiation temperature (SIT) is a primary determinant of packaging line throughput on vertical form–fill–seal machines. This work compared cast films produced from four mLLDPE resins differing in comonomer type (1-butene, 1-hexene, or 1-octene) at constant density (0.918 g/cm³) and melt flow index (2.0 g/10 min). Films of 40 µm nominal thickness were extruded on a laboratory cast-film line and sealed over a 90–135 °C range at 0.3 N/mm² and 0.5 s dwell time. Seal strength was measured by 180° peel on a tensile tester. The 1-octene grade yielded the lowest SIT (97 °C) and a plateau seal strength of 28 N/25 mm, compared to 108 °C and 22 N/25 mm for the 1-butene grade. DSC melting profiles correlated well with the observed SIT differences. Hot-tack measurements at 500 mm/s jaw separation confirmed that 1-octene resins provide a 14 °C wider hot-tack window, relevant for high-speed filling lines.

A cross-border collaboration between the Faculty of Technology Novi Sad and the Department of Plastics Technology at Budapest University of Technology, co-funded under Interreg IPA. The project addressed gaps in the regional packaging film industry by developing shared test protocols for heat-seal quality assessment and transferring extensional rheology measurement competence to the Serbian side. Grbić led Work Package 2, covering heat-seal and hot-tack testing protocol harmonisation and the comparative study of 180° peel versus burst test methods. Joint workshops were held in both Novi Sad and Budapest. A shared database of polymer melt rheology and seal-performance data was compiled and made available to packaging SMEs in both countries.

Grbić has expressed a preference for collaborations that can access production-scale extrusion equipment, as the laboratory cast-film line is limited to 45 mm screw diameter and cannot replicate all industrial conditions. He is not currently on sabbatical and is available for new project discussions.

A two-dimensional finite-difference model was developed to simulate transient heat and moisture transfer in a sealed steel enclosure containing a heat-dissipating printed circuit board. The model couples Fourier conduction through the walls with Fickian vapour diffusion and accounts for condensation on internal surfaces when local temperature drops below the dew point. Internal heat generation was set at 5 W, representing a typical low-power controller unit. Simulations were run for a 24-hour diurnal ambient profile representative of a Pannonian autumn day. Results showed that condensation first occurred on the lower half of the front panel after approximately 17 minutes of rapid external temperature drop at −1.2 °C/min. Increasing the initial internal air volume by 30 % by deepening the enclosure reduced condensation onset time by only 4 minutes, while adding a 2-g silica-gel desiccant delayed onset by 38 minutes. The model was validated against thermocouple and humidity logger measurements from a physical enclosure subjected to a controlled temperature ramp in a climate chamber.

Four commercial IP54-rated steel enclosures were instrumented with capacitive humidity sensors inside and outside, and temperature sensors at the wall mid-plane and external surface. They were mounted on a south-facing outdoor test rack in Novi Sad from March to October 2013. Internal relative humidity tracked external daily temperature cycles with a phase lag of approximately 3–4 hours. Total cumulative moisture ingress over the measurement period ranged from 4.2 to 7.8 g per enclosure, varying with seal type and mounting orientation. A one-dimensional transient diffusion model driven by measured vapour-pressure gradients reproduced the seasonal trend with a mean absolute error below 12 % when an effective diffusivity of 3.1 × 10⁻¹² m²/s was used for the compressed gasket region. The model indicates that horizontal lid orientation with a downward-facing seal gap reduces ingress by approximately 35 % compared with vertical orientation.

Foam-in-place (FIP) polyurethane gaskets applied to twelve sheet-metal electrical cabinet covers were compared with die-cut EPDM strips on twelve matched cabinets over a 36-month outdoor exposure period in a semi-urban environment near Novi Sad. Both cabinet populations were inspected every six months for visual defects, and sample gaskets were removed annually for laboratory compression-set and Shore A testing. FIP gaskets maintained lower compression-set values (mean 17 % at 36 months) compared with EPDM strips (mean 29 %), and showed less dimensional variability across the bead cross-section. However, four FIP samples exhibited adhesion loss at corners after 24 months when substrate surface preparation was below the specified cleanliness grade. Internal humidity loggers showed that cabinets with FIP gaskets experienced 11 % fewer condensation events over the monitoring period. Cost-benefit analysis incorporating material, application labour, and seal replacement is also presented.

Fourteen silicone O-rings were removed from photovoltaic string combiner boxes that had been in service for approximately five years at three sites across Vojvodina. Visual inspection, Shore A hardness testing, tensile testing, thermogravimetric analysis, and SEM imaging were performed on extracted seals and compared with unused reference samples from the same production lot. Average hardness increased by 9 Shore A units, elongation at break decreased by 31 %, and TGA showed a 2.1 % mass loss in the 200–400 °C range attributed to low-molecular-weight siloxane volatilisation. SEM images revealed surface crazing on seals from south-facing installations, consistent with UV-ozone degradation. Correlation analysis showed that enclosures with measured internal humidity above 75 % RH for more than 400 cumulative hours per year had a significantly higher incidence of corrosion on copper busbars, linking seal degradation to electrical component failure.
Thermal-gradient-driven breathing in partially sealed enclosures: pressure differential measurements and implications for seal loading

MOISTMOD targets the development of validated computational models for predicting moisture accumulation and condensation onset in sealed outdoor enclosures used in low-voltage electrical distribution infrastructure. The project combines laboratory climate-chamber experiments with two-dimensional coupled heat-moisture FEM simulations. A parametric study covering five enclosure sizes, three gasket materials, and four regional climate profiles is being conducted. An open-access Python-based tool for condensation-onset prediction is under development. The project involves collaboration with a meteorological data provider and an enclosure manufacturer. One postdoctoral researcher and two doctoral students are supported under the project.

The project set up a networked outdoor test rack with 24 instrumented enclosures across three sites in Vojvodina to collect simultaneous internal humidity, temperature, and condensation-event data over 30 months. Gasket specimens from each enclosure were retrieved at 10-month intervals for laboratory characterisation. The data collected formed the basis for the regression model relating enclosure configuration and gland fill ratio to condensation frequency, and provided field-correlation reference points for the accelerated ageing protocol developed subsequently. Two M.Sc. theses and one Ph.D. thesis were completed within the project scope.

NBR gaskets of two hardness grades (50 and 70 Shore A) were subjected to repeated immersion in distilled water at 25 °C for 8 hours followed by drying at 60 °C for 16 hours, simulating dew-cycle condensation, for up to 90 cycles. Mass uptake, dimensional change in thickness, and compression-set were tracked after every 15 cycles. The softer 50 Shore A grade reached a water uptake plateau of 4.8 % by mass after 45 cycles, accompanied by a 1.7 % thickness increase. The 70 Shore A grade showed 2.9 % uptake and 0.9 % thickness increase. Compressive stress relaxation tests after the final cycle showed that both grades lost 22–27 % of initial contact-force capacity. Hardness measurements after cycling indicated slight softening (−3 to −5 Shore A units) for both grades. The data suggest that groove-depth tolerances should be re-evaluated when NBR seals are used in condensation-prone environments.

Six aluminium flange specimens were machined to surface roughness values Ra between 0.8 µm and 6.3 µm, and paired with 2-mm NBR and EPDM flat gaskets at clamping pressures of 1, 2, and 4 MPa. Helium leak tests were conducted at an internal overpressure of 0.5 bar. Leak rate increased by more than one order of magnitude when Ra changed from 1.6 µm to 6.3 µm at the lowest clamping pressure. At 4 MPa clamping, NBR showed a 40 % lower leak rate than EPDM on rougher surfaces, attributed to its higher elastic modulus enabling better micro-asperity conformity at elevated contact stress. A contact-mechanics model based on Greenwood–Williamson statistics was used to predict effective contact area and showed reasonable agreement with measured leak rates. Practical guidelines for flange finishing standards in low-preload enclosure assemblies are proposed.

The heat transfer coefficient (HTC) between polymer melt and mould steel during the filling and packing stages is a poorly characterised boundary condition that strongly influences warpage predictions. This study systematically varied the interfacial HTC from 1000 to 10 000 W/m²K in a commercial process simulation environment for a PA6 box-shaped part (80 × 60 × 30 mm, 2.5 mm wall) and quantified the resulting spread in predicted warpage and residual stress distributions. Warpage at the open rim varied by up to 0.38 mm (factor of 2.4) over the HTC range, whereas residual stresses at mid-wall varied by less than 6%. An inverse identification procedure using CMM warpage measurements from 20 experimental parts at two mould temperatures was used to back-calculate effective HTC values. Identified HTC values were 2 400 ± 310 W/m²K at 40 °C mould temperature and 1 850 ± 260 W/m²K at 70 °C mould temperature. Recommendations for standardising HTC calibration in simulation workflows are given.

This study examines how packing pressure level affects the degree of crystallinity distribution and final part warpage in polyamide 6 (PA6) flat components (100 × 100 × 2 mm). Experiments were performed on a 60-tonne hydraulic injection moulding machine at packing pressures ranging from 40 to 100 MPa in steps of 20 MPa. Crystallinity was measured by DSC on specimens cut from five through-thickness positions. Warpage was quantified with a coordinate measuring machine at a 5 × 5 grid of points. Higher packing pressure increased average crystallinity from 28% to 36% but reduced warpage from 0.41 mm to 0.17 mm due to reduced volumetric shrinkage. A commercial process simulation code was used to model the crystallisation kinetics using an Avrami-type model with parameters fitted to the DSC data. Simulated crystallinity gradients matched measured gradients with a mean absolute error of 2.3 percentage points across all packing conditions.
Sensitivity of warpage predictions to mould heat transfer coefficient: a parametric study for polyamide 6 box-shaped parts

Thick-walled PP optical mounting brackets (nominal wall thickness 8 mm) for automotive lighting assemblies require tight dimensional tolerances and are particularly susceptible to warpage driven by differential cooling between the cavity and core sides of the mould. This study investigates the relationship between the cooling rate asymmetry and final warpage for four mould configurations with varying cavity-to-core mould temperature ratios (ΔT = 0, 10, 20, 30 °C; cavity side always colder). Warpage was measured on 15 parts per condition using a structured-light scanner with 0.02 mm point accuracy. Differential cooling induced a systematic bowing, with warpage increasing from 0.12 mm at ΔT = 0 to 0.91 mm at ΔT = 30 °C. Thermomechanical simulations captured this trend with a maximum error of 0.11 mm. Through-thickness crystallinity measurements confirmed that the core-side crystallinity exceeded the cavity-side value by up to 6 percentage points at ΔT = 30 °C, directly contributing to differential shrinkage.

Aleksandar Bošković received his Dipl.Ing. degree in Mechanical Engineering from the University of Novi Sad in 2004 and his PhD from the same institution in 2011, with a thesis on residual stress formation in injection-moulded semi-crystalline thermoplastics. He was appointed Assistant Professor in 2012 and promoted to Associate Professor in 2018 within the Department of Mechanical Engineering at the Faculty of Technical Sciences. His research group focuses on coupled thermomechanical simulation of polymer processing, particularly predicting warpage, residual stresses, and optimising mould cooling systems for semi-crystalline materials such as polyamide and polypropylene. He teaches courses in Machine Elements and Polymer Processing Technology. The group works primarily with commercial FEA and injection moulding simulation packages, and has access to a materials testing laboratory with DSC, tensile testing frames, and coordinate measuring equipment for warpage validation.

Two-component injection moulding of polypropylene (PP) substrate and polyamide 6 (PA6) overmould was studied with respect to residual stress development and warpage. The process involves sequential injection into a rotary mould; the PP substrate cools partially before PA6 is injected over it. A sequential thermomechanical FE simulation was implemented to capture stress accumulation in both materials and at the interface. The PP thermoviscoelastic material model and PA6 crystallisation model were taken from previous calibrated studies. Simulations were compared against CMM warpage measurements on 40 two-component plaques (160 × 80 mm) produced at two substrate pre-cooling times (8 and 15 s). Predicted warpage matched measurements within 0.09 mm for the 15 s pre-cooling case and within 0.21 mm for the 8 s case, where incomplete solidification of the substrate introduced additional uncertainty. Interfacial stress concentrations are identified as a potential delamination risk at sharp edges.

The project addresses a gap in predictive capability for residual stresses and warpage in injection-moulded semi-crystalline thermoplastics. The core activities include calibration of crystallisation kinetics models for PA6 and PP at industrially relevant cooling rates, implementation of a fully coupled thermomechanical simulation chain, and systematic experimental validation using in-mould sensors and post-ejection CMM and structured-light scanning. The project team of four researchers from the Faculty of Technical Sciences collaborates with the Faculty of Technology Novi Sad for DSC characterisation and with partners at the University of Maribor for material modelling. By the end of the project, a validated simulation workflow and a material parameter database will be made available as open data for Serbian polymer processing industry users.

Prefers collaborative arrangements where industrial partners can supply moulded test parts and process data; the laboratory is not equipped for in-house injection moulding production. Primary simulation tools are commercially licensed, so any collaborative project involving proprietary simulation environments would need a separate software access agreement.

PERMTEMP aimed to produce a systematically collected reference dataset of temperature-dependent oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour permeability for ten commercially relevant polyolefin film grades, covering the range 5–50 °C. Arrhenius activation energies and pre-exponential factors were determined by least-squares regression on multi-temperature OTR and WVTR datasets. The dataset was made available to Serbian food-industry companies through a technical report and an online spreadsheet tool for shelf-life estimation. The project also calibrated the Faculty of Technology permeability laboratory instruments against certified reference films, establishing a documented calibration protocol that remains in use.

Commercially metallised cast polypropylene (CPP) films with aluminium optical densities ranging from 2.1 to 3.6 were characterised for OTR and WVTR immediately after production and after 90-day ambient storage. At optical density 3.6, OTR was 4 cm³/(m²·day·bar) and WVTR was 0.18 g/(m²·day) immediately after metallisation. After 90 days these rose by 18 % and 24 % respectively. SEM cross-sections and atomic force microscopy revealed microcrack formation in the aluminium layer, with crack density correlating with ageing-induced OTR increase (R² = 0.87). Corona pre-treatment level (measured by contact angle) did not significantly affect initial barrier but reduced the rate of crack formation during ageing by approximately 30 %. The study provides quantitative ageing coefficients applicable to worst-case shelf-life calculations for hermetically sealed snack products.

Oxygen transmission rate was measured on commercial and laboratory-cast LLDPE films of three densities (0.918, 0.924, 0.932 g/cm³) across a temperature range of 5 °C to 50 °C. Arrhenius plots were constructed from OTR data collected at seven temperature points; activation energies for permeation ranged from 28.4 to 41.7 kJ/mol and increased with film density, in line with reduced chain mobility at higher crystallinity. Positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS) performed in collaboration with a partner institution provided free-volume hole radius estimates of 0.26–0.31 nm at 23 °C. A positive correlation (R² = 0.91) between hole radius and permeability coefficient was observed. Pre-exponential diffusivity factors derived from the Arrhenius fits correlated with crystallinity index from DSC. These data are intended as reference parameters for shelf-life modelling of chilled food products stored at variable temperatures.

Snežana Puzović completed her undergraduate and master's studies in Chemical Engineering at the Faculty of Technology, University of Novi Sad, graduating in 1998 and 2001 respectively, before receiving her PhD in Materials Engineering from the same institution in 2007. She joined the Department of Materials Engineering as an assistant professor in 2008 and was promoted to full professor in 2019. Her research group focuses on the transport properties of polyolefin-based multilayer and mono-material packaging films, with particular attention to oxygen and water vapour transmission rates across temperature gradients, crystallinity effects, and the design of EVOH-free high-barrier systems compatible with mechanical recycling streams. She teaches courses in Polymer Materials and Packaging Technology. The group operates a dedicated permeability testing laboratory equipped with OX-TRAN and PERMATRAN-W instruments, DSC, FTIR-ATR, and a bench-scale film coextrusion line.

Biaxially oriented polypropylene (BOPP) films prepared at draw ratios of 5×5 to 9×9 were characterised for oxygen transmission rate (OTR) using a coulometric sensor method at 23 °C and 0 % relative humidity. Wide-angle X-ray scattering confirmed an increase in crystallinity from 42 % to 61 % with rising draw ratio. OTR values decreased from 1840 to 890 cm³/(m²·day·bar) over the same range. DSC measurements showed that lamellar thickness, as estimated by the Thomson–Gibbs equation, increased from 8.2 to 14.7 nm. A linear correlation was established between the reciprocal of lamellar thickness and OTR, consistent with a tortuous-path diffusion model. FTIR-ATR band ratios at 998/973 cm⁻¹ were used as an independent crystallinity index and agreed within 4 % with WAXS results. The findings provide quantitative guidance for process optimisation of BOPP films where oxygen barrier is the primary constraint.

A coextruded film comprising two polyolefin outer plies, two tie-layer plies based on maleic-anhydride-grafted polyethylene, and a central ply of amorphous polyethylene terephthalate of 15–35 µm thickness. The structure achieves an oxygen transmission rate below 50 cm³/(m²·day·bar) at 23 °C while maintaining mechanical recyclability when blended with standard polyethylene recyclate streams at up to 10 % by mass contamination. The claimed invention covers the composition ranges and extrusion temperature windows that prevent crystallisation of the PET ply during processing. A dataset of 214 production batches of three-layer LLDPE/mLLDPE/LLDPE cast films (40–80 µm) collected over 18 months from an industrial film producer was analysed to establish a statistical relationship between pinhole density (measured by electrical discharge imaging) and OTR. Pinhole density ranged from 0 to 8 pinholes/m² and OTR ranged from 1600 to 3100 cm³/(m²·day·bar). A linear regression model explained 61 % of OTR variance (R² = 0.61) using pinhole density as the sole predictor; inclusion of film thickness, extrusion speed and melt temperature raised R² to 0.79. Films with zero pinholes showed an OTR range of 1580–1980 cm³/(m²·day·bar), confirming that pinhole-free conditions alone do not guarantee low OTR. These findings are communicated to the production partner as a quality-control decision tool. The methodology is generic and applicable to other thin film geometries.

Alternating layers of poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) (PDADMAC) and poly(sodium 4-styrenesulfonate) (PSS) were deposited on corona-treated LLDPE substrates via dip-coating at pH 4.0 and ionic strength 0.1 M NaCl. Films with 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 bilayers were produced and OTR measured at 23 °C and 50 % RH. OTR decreased from 1720 cm³/(m²·day·bar) for uncoated LLDPE to 210 cm³/(m²·day·bar) at 20 bilayers; total coating thickness was 380 nm by profilometry. Adhesion of the coating was assessed by tape-peel and cross-cut tests; failure occurred at the coating–substrate interface for samples with fewer than 8 bilayers, suggesting inadequate corona treatment recovery. Humid ageing at 85 % RH for 14 days caused an OTR increase of 35 % at 20 bilayers. The coating approach is positioned as an EVOH-free route to moderate oxygen barrier on flexible polyolefin substrates.

A two-dimensional finite-volume model of moisture and heat transport was developed for a generic polycarbonate housing representative of handheld electronic devices. The domain included the polymer shell, an internal air cavity of 38 cm³, and a printed circuit board heat source. Boundary conditions followed a 24-hour ambient cycle between 5 °C and 35 °C at 60–90 % relative humidity, representative of coastal storage conditions. The dew-point margin at the coldest internal surface was tracked over 72 simulated hours. For a housing wall thickness of 2 mm with no desiccant, the dew-point margin dropped below zero during the cooling phase at hour 14, predicting condensation on the board. Adding a 0.5 g silica gel insert raised the margin to +1.8 °C at the same instant. Model sensitivity to polycarbonate vapour diffusivity was assessed over a ±30 % range; the condensation-onset time varied by ±2.1 hours. The numerical approach is validated against laboratory cycling tests using thermocouples and a miniature humidity probe placed inside the cavity.

A coupled simulation workflow was developed to map condensation risk on internal surfaces of wall-mounted outdoor plastic housings under winter conditions. A three-dimensional steady-state CFD model computed the internal temperature distribution accounting for natural convection and wall conduction; the resulting surface temperature field was then passed as a boundary condition to a vapour diffusion model that predicted local relative humidity and dew-point margin at each surface node. A 6-litre ABS housing with a 20 W internal heat source was simulated at external temperatures of −10 °C, 0 °C, and 10 °C at 90 % external relative humidity with a seal permeance of 3.5 × 10⁻¹² kg/(m²·s·Pa). At −10 °C, 14 % of the internal wall area showed a negative dew-point margin; this reduced to 3 % at 0 °C and to zero at 10 °C. A redesign placing the heat source at the geometric bottom of the housing eliminated the negative-margin area at −10 °C. The workflow is implemented in open-source tools and requires less than 4 hours of computation time on a workstation.

This project developed a prototype wireless sensor node small enough to be enclosed permanently inside a standard IP65 cabinet, transmitting temperature and humidity readings via LoRaWAN. Sabo's group led the work package on enclosure climate modelling and sensor placement optimisation, using CFD and hygrothermal simulations to identify locations within the cabinet where the sensor reading is most representative of the condensation-risk state of the enclosure. Two candidate sensor positions were evaluated against a 24-thermocouple reference dataset; the recommended position reduced the root-mean-square error in condensation-onset prediction from 4.1 hours to 1.3 hours compared with an unguided placement. The project partnered with an electronics engineering group for sensor hardware and firmware development.

Twelve steel electrical cabinets installed in four unheated substations in Vojvodina were instrumented with internal and external temperature–humidity loggers over a 14-month period spanning two winters. Internal relative humidity exceeded 85 % for more than 480 hours per year in cabinets without anti-condensation heaters, with the longest continuous exceedance episode lasting 61 hours. A lumped-parameter hygrothermal model driven by measured exterior boundary conditions reproduced the measured internal humidity with a root-mean-square error of 3.2 percentage points. Model calibration identified the dominant vapour pathway as the cable entry glands rather than the door gasket, accounting for approximately 68 % of total vapour ingress. Anti-condensation heater power requirements derived from the model range from 6 W to 22 W depending on cabinet volume. Recommendations for gland specification and heater sizing are given.

Svetlana Sabo received her Diploma Engineer degree in Mechanical Engineering from the University of Novi Sad in 1998 and her PhD from the same institution in 2005, with a thesis on moisture transport across elastomeric seals in low-pressure enclosures. She joined the Department of Mechanical Engineering at the Faculty of Technical Sciences as an Assistant Professor in 2006 and was promoted to Full Professor in 2018. Her research group focuses on thermal-fluid behaviour inside sealed cavities, with particular emphasis on hygrothermal modelling, condensation onset prediction, and the influence of seal geometry and vapour permeability on internal dew-point conditions. She teaches courses in fluid mechanics, heat transfer, and machine elements. The group operates a climate-controlled test chamber, a gravimetric vapour sorption analyser, and a suite of infrared thermography equipment.

This book chapter reviews the physical mechanisms governing moisture behaviour in mechanically sealed enclosures, covering vapour diffusion through seal materials, convective moisture transport in internal air volumes, and sorption on interior polymer surfaces. The chapter presents one-dimensional and two-dimensional analytical solutions for steady-state and transient vapour transport in simple geometries, followed by a discussion of finite-element and finite-volume implementations for complex enclosure shapes. A worked example demonstrates the prediction of condensation onset time for a 2-litre aluminium housing sealed with a silicone gasket subjected to a step change in external relative humidity from 50 % to 95 %. The chapter also addresses the coupling between thermal and hygric calculations, noting conditions under which decoupled analysis is acceptable (Biot number for vapour transfer below 0.1). Measurement techniques for validating hygrothermal models, including gravimetric permeability testing, capacitive sensing, and fibre-optic dew-point measurement, are described.

A hygrothermal model of a polyphthalamide (PPA) junction box used in crystalline silicon photovoltaic modules was subjected to a global sensitivity analysis using the Sobol variance decomposition method. Nine input parameters were varied: gasket vapour permeability, gasket cross-section width, groove surface roughness, internal air volume, internal polymer sorption isotherm slope, external temperature amplitude, external humidity amplitude, solar irradiance-driven temperature offset, and potting compound surface area. Each parameter was sampled over physically realistic ranges drawn from the literature and from in-house measurements. A total of 18 432 model evaluations were performed. The first-order Sobol index for the time to condensation onset was dominated by gasket vapour permeability (S₁ = 0.41) and external humidity amplitude (S₁ = 0.28). Grove surface roughness had a smaller but non-negligible contribution (S₁ = 0.09). The analysis identifies gasket material selection and installation surface finish as the most impactful design levers for extending the condensation-free service life of PV junction boxes.

A simulation workflow is described that takes hourly meteorological station data (dry-bulb temperature and relative humidity) as its sole external boundary condition and predicts the time-history of the dew-point margin on the coldest internal surface of a sealed outdoor enclosure. The workflow chains a thermal resistance–capacitance model of the enclosure wall with a lumped vapour mass-balance model and a local surface temperature correction derived from a short CFD pre-computation. It was applied to three years of hourly data (2021–2023) from the Rimski Šančevi meteorological station near Novi Sad for three enclosure configurations: unheated ABS 1-litre, unheated aluminium 4-litre, and aluminium 4-litre with 10 W anti-condensation heater. The workflow predicted that the unheated ABS enclosure experienced 312 condensation-onset events over three years; the unheated aluminium enclosure experienced 94, and the heated aluminium enclosure experienced zero. Predictions were validated against a 12-month data set from four instrumented enclosures deployed at the same station, with onset event counts matching to within 8 %.

Optical devices assembled in factories at relative humidity levels of 30 %, 50 %, and 70 % were modelled and tested to quantify the long-term internal moisture level reached after hermetic sealing. A one-dimensional mass-balance model predicts that the asymptotic internal humidity is determined by the initial air charge, the internal surface sorption capacity of polymer components, and the slow permeation through glass-to-metal adhesive joints. For an assembly humidity of 70 %, the model predicts a post-sealing equilibrium internal relative humidity of 22 % at 20 °C; at 30 % assembly humidity this falls to 9 %. Twelve laboratory assemblies per condition, sealed with a tin-indium solder alloy joint, were placed in a climate chamber and monitored via a fibre-optic dew-point sensor for 18 months. Predictions and measurements agree within 4 percentage points. The study underpins a factory specification of maximum 45 % assembly-room humidity to maintain the internal level below 15 % over a 10-year service life.

Vapour permeability was measured for EPDM, silicone, and thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) seal materials in unaged condition and after accelerated thermal ageing (100 °C, 1000 hours) and UV ageing (1.0 W/m² at 340 nm, 500 hours) in accordance with ISO 4892-2. Gravimetric cup tests at 23 °C and 85 % relative humidity differential were conducted on three specimens per material per ageing condition. EPDM permeability increased by 12 % after thermal ageing and by 8 % after UV ageing relative to the unaged baseline. Silicone showed no statistically significant change after thermal ageing but a 19 % increase after UV ageing. TPU exhibited the largest sensitivity, with permeability increasing by 34 % after thermal ageing and 27 % after UV ageing, accompanied by visible surface crazing and a 15 % reduction in hardness. Shore A hardness, tensile elongation at break, and infrared spectroscopy were used to characterise degradation mechanisms. The results indicate that TPU is not recommended for long-service-life outdoor enclosures exposed to solar radiation.

A central composite design was used to map the effect of barrel temperature (120–160 °C), screw speed (80–200 rpm), and sunflower protein concentrate content (0–25 wt%) on the mechanical and barrier properties of blown films produced from the extruded blends via a subsequent film blowing step. Seventeen experimental runs yielded response surfaces for tensile strength, elongation at break, Young's modulus, water vapour transmission rate (WVTR), and oxygen transmission rate (OTR). Tensile strength ranged from 7.2 to 16.8 MPa across the design space; OTR varied from 180 to 620 cm³·m⁻²·day⁻¹·bar⁻¹. Optimal conditions identified by desirability function (maximum strength and minimum OTR) were 148 °C, 145 rpm, and 18 wt% protein. At the optimum, predicted and experimental values agreed within 6%. Specific mechanical energy was modelled as a secondary response and found to increase linearly with screw speed but to show a quadratic relationship with protein content, with a minimum near 12 wt% attributed to lubrication effects of denatured protein at low concentration.

Polyetherimide (PEI) is used in precision-fit diagnostic device components where dimensional tolerances of ±0.02 mm or tighter are required. This work tracks dimensional changes in injection-moulded PEI discs and pins stored in sealed packaging at three relative humidity levels (30%, 60%, and 90%) over 18 months. CMM measurements at six-month intervals show that at 90% RH, average diameter growth reached 0.015 mm after 18 months, representing 75% of the maximum allowable tolerance. Moisture uptake at 90% RH reached 1.2 wt%, consistent with literature values for unfilled PEI. Specimens stored at 30% RH showed negligible dimensional change (<0.003 mm). A linear predictive model relating absorbed moisture to dimensional deviation, validated against independent specimens, is presented with 95% confidence intervals. The study provides evidence to support the use of desiccant packaging with a humidity indicator below 40% RH for long shelf-life storage of PEI diagnostic components.

Selective laser sintered (SLS) polyamide 12 specimens were subjected to 10 repeated cycles of moisture absorption (95% RH, 37 °C, 7 days) and desorption (23 °C, 50% RH, 7 days) prior to fatigue testing. A control group was tested in the dry-as-built condition. Tension–tension fatigue tests (R = 0.1, 1 Hz, 37 °C) were performed. The cyclic hygroscopic treatment reduced fatigue life at 40 MPa by 38% compared with the dry control group. Micro-CT imaging performed before and after the hygroscopic cycling revealed enlargement of interlayer porosity, with mean pore diameter increasing from 48 µm to 67 µm. Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) showed a reduction in storage modulus of 12% and an increase in the loss tangent peak area of 18% after hygroscopic cycling, indicating increased viscoelastic energy dissipation per cycle. The findings are relevant to the growing use of SLS-printed PA12 in patient-specific surgical guides and low-load orthopaedic ancillaries.

Three accelerated ageing protocols for thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) catheter tubing segments are compared: elevated temperature immersion (70 °C in phosphate-buffered saline), combined UV/humidity exposure (UVA, 0.76 W/m², 50% RH), and real-time ageing at 23 °C/50% RH over 52 weeks. Fatigue life under cyclic bending (displacement-controlled, 1 Hz, 180° bend radius) was measured for each protocol at nominal ageing equivalents of 6, 12, 24, and 52 weeks. The elevated temperature protocol was the most aggressive: fatigue life after 24-week equivalent ageing dropped to 42% of the initial value. Molecular weight (GPC), hardness (Shore A), and elongation at break were measured alongside fatigue data. Arrhenius correlation between the 70 °C and 23 °C datasets yielded an activation energy of 84 kJ/mol, within the range expected for hydrolytic degradation of polyester-based TPU. The UV/humidity protocol produced divergent results not predictable from the thermal model, suggesting a different degradation mechanism relevant only to external device surfaces.

This paper investigates whether DMA measurements—specifically storage modulus E′, loss modulus E″, and the loss tangent tan δ recorded at 1, 10, and 100 Hz—can serve as rapid non-destructive predictors of residual fatigue life in humidity-aged polymer specimens without performing full fatigue tests. Four materials were studied: PA6, PA66-GF30, POM-C, and PEEK, each aged at 85% RH and 37 °C for 0, 4, 8, 16, and 32 weeks. DMA signatures were correlated with fatigue lives measured at a fixed stress amplitude of 40% of the tensile strength for each material–ageing combination (n = 8 per data point). For PA6 and PA66-GF30, tan δ at 1 Hz showed the strongest correlation with residual fatigue life (Pearson r = −0.91 and −0.87 respectively). POM-C and PEEK showed weaker correlations (r = −0.61 and −0.54), consistent with their low moisture uptake limiting the DMA-detectable change. A simple regression-based screening criterion using tan δ thresholds is proposed and its applicability limits are discussed.
